cards.explanation: The answer is that the godly and the faithful have vanished. That's the whole reason David cries out. He says "…the godly are no more; the faithful have vanished from among men." He doesn't open with small talk, friends. He opens with "Help, O LORD…" and then lays out the trouble.

The word is "lie." David says "They lie to one another…" and it sits right alongside the flattering lips and the double heart. The words sound sweet, but the heart behind them isn't matching. I think that's what makes a double heart so hard to spot.

The answer is that David asks the LORD to cut them off. He prays, "May the LORD cut off all flattering lips and every boastful tongue." Notice, friends, he brings it to the LORD in prayer. He asks the LORD to do the cutting off.
The answer is their tongues. They say, "With our tongues we will prevail." That's the boast, plain and simple. It comes right after David prays about flattering lips and every boastful tongue.

The answer is False. The smooth talkers say the opposite. Their words are "We own our lips—who can be our master?" They're asking who could possibly be their master, friends. The very next verse is the LORD speaking.

The answer is True, and it's a big moment. After the smooth talkers finish bragging, the LORD says, "…I will now arise…" in verse 5. The psalm has been David talking, and then the LORD speaks for Himself. Those boasters said nobody could be their master, and then the LORD speaks.

The answer is the oppressed and the needy. The LORD says, "For the cause of the oppressed and for the groaning of the needy, I will now arise…" He hears the groaning, friends. He also says, "I will bring safety to him who yearns."

The word is "flawless." David says, "The words of the LORD are flawless, like silver refined in a furnace…" Flawless means nothing is wrong with them. After a whole psalm about slippery, lying words, that's a big contrast.

The answer is that the LORD will keep us and guard us forever. David says, "You, O LORD, will keep us; You will forever guard us from this generation." He's talking right to the LORD now. The crowd around him is lying and boasting, but his hope is in the One who keeps and guards.

The answer is False. The last line says the opposite, friends. David ends with "The wicked wander freely, and vileness is exalted among men." The wicked are still out there. He sings the whole psalm straight, and he doesn't tie the ending up with a bow.
